**I. Introduction & Citation**

Electronic circuits never perform the same way twice because every component has small variations in its real value compared to its nominal rating. These differences, along with environmental factors such as temperature changes, can cause circuits to drift from their ideal behavior. In practical designs, especially those that rely on voltage thresholds or timing, small variations can lead to noticeable performance differences. Understanding how sensitive a circuit is to these variations is an important part of reliable design.

Monte Carlo simulation is a tool that helps evaluate how component tolerances and temperature changes affect circuit performance. Instead of analyzing one perfect version of a circuit, Monte Carlo runs the same simulation many times while randomly changing component values within their tolerance ranges. This creates a realistic picture of how the circuit might behave in real-world conditions. The results can be plotted as histograms or statistical distributions that show the expected range of circuit performance.

For this project, a PWM comparator circuit was designed and tested in LTSpice. It is planned to make the numeric micron troller air quality to be a PWM signal as it is faster and more resilient to noise than sending a DC voltage. The circuit has two LEDs to provide a visual indication of the comparison result: when the PWM duty cycle is below 50%, green LED 2 lights up; when it is above 50%, red LED 1 turns on; representing good and poor air quality, respectively. The goal of the analysis is to determine how component tolerances and temperature variations affect the threshold voltage where the LEDs switch states. By applying Monte Carlo and temperature sweeps, the stability and robustness of the circuit can be evaluated under realistic manufacturing and environmental variations.

**II. Schematic and Description**

_A. Schematic_

![A computer screen shot of a diagram

AI-generated content may be incorrect.](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 1. Air Quality Status Indicator via LEDs

_B. Description_

The air quality status indicator circuit operates by converting a PWM signal, whose duty cycle represents air pollution level (20% and 60% for testing), into a corresponding DC voltage that can be compared against a reference threshold. The PWM input from source V1 passes through a low-pass filter designed for a center frequency of 100Hz, composed of R1, L1, and C1. This filter smooths the pulse into an average voltage proportional to air quality: a higher duty cycle produces a higher voltage, indicating poorer air conditions. Furthermore, the inductor L1 was added to increase the quality factor and improve the 10-90 rise time from 5ms to 0.2ms. This filtered signal drives the transistor stage built around Q1, which buffers and amplifies the signal for comparison. Transistors Q2 through Q4, along with diode D1, form a biasing and reference network that establishes a stable threshold voltage roughly corresponding to a 50% duty cycle or at half of the microcontroller supply voltage of 3.3 volts. The voltage follower op-amp U1 functions as a buffer. This helps to separate and provide isolation to the branches of the pullup and pulldown LEDs. When the measured air quality duty cycle exceeds the reference threshold of 50%, indicating degraded air, the 7400 NAND output goes low, turning on the red LED (DLO) through pullup resistor R5 to signal poor air quality. Conversely, when the air is clean and the duty cycle is below the threshold of 50%, the 7400 NAND output goes high, activating the green LED (DHI) through pulldown resistor R6. This provides a clear visual indication of environmental conditions, green for good air quality, and red for bad air.

The creator of this circuit was Ryan Neimi with help from lab work done in EE449 with Steve Dunton and from EE347 with Dr. Jin. The averaging filter was learned in EE409 while studying usages of phase-locked loops, whereas the buffering and pullup/pulldown networks were learned during circuits 2. Testing and finalizing the filter inductor value was done through experimentation in LTSpice after initially choosing an RC value for 102Hz while using common 10% values for components.

**III. Design Specifications**

The purpose of this circuit is to determine whether an incoming 100 kHz, 3.3 V PWM signal is above or below a 50% duty cycle and to display this state using two LEDs. The LED forward voltages provide a clear, quantitative metric for verifying correct operation.

Design Specification: When driven with a 100 kHz, 3.3 V PWM input, the circuit shall reliably identify whether the duty cycle is greater or less than 50%. For duty cycles greater than 50%, LED1 (pull-up LED) shall turn ON with a forward voltage of ≥ 600 mV, while LED2 (pull-down LED) shall remain OFF with forward voltage < 600 mV. For duty cycles less than 50%, LED2 shall turn ON with forward voltage ≥ 600 mV, and LED1 shall remain OFF with forward voltage < 600 mV, measured after steady-state settling.

A 60% and 20% PWM waveform was selected for testing because it clearly represents the "greater-than-50%" and "lower-than-50%" case. This allows verification of the ON/OFF thresholds for both LEDs while subjecting the circuit to realistic component tolerances and temperature variation from -25 °C to 85 °C.

In summary, the circuit must satisfy:

- Threshold accuracy: Correct LED selection for >50% or <50% duty cycle
- Voltage criteria: LED ON ≥ 600 mV, LED OFF < 600 mV
- Robustness: Behavior must remain correct across component tolerances and -25 °C to 85 °C

**PWM Signal Generation:**

A PWM signal is a square wave whose duty cycle represents the fraction of time the signal is high. In this circuit, the PWM duty cycle determines which LED should illuminate. A 1 MHz, 3.3 V PWM input is used, where duty cycles above or below 50% map directly to the LED output states.

Low-Pass Filtering: To interpret the PWM duty cycle as an analog level, the signal is passed through a second-order RLC low-pass filter made from a 30 Ω resistor, a 2.2 mH inductor, and a 10 µF capacitor. This filter removes the 100 kHz switching harmonics and produces a smooth DC voltage proportional to the PWM duty cycle. Its cutoff frequency is approximately 1.07 kHz, much lower than the PWM frequency, ensuring effective filtering and a stable average voltage for comparison.

7400 NAND Stage: The 7400LC NAND gate has a VOH of 3.3V and a VOL of 0.65V=VBE. The midpoint swing is 1.65=VDD/2. The filtered voltage is then fed into a buffer, allowing for isolation between the pullup and pulldown branch. In the pullup branch, only if the NAND output is low and input is high will the red LED turn on, or when the duty cycle exceeds 50%. Conversely, in the pulldown branch, only if the NAND output is high and input is low will the green LED turn on, or when the duty cycle is below 50%. The LEDs are both assumed to have a forward bias voltage of 0.6V; in reality the green LED will likely have a higher bias voltage than the red LED. Lastly, the transients are assumed to die quickly - the first 0.2ms could display the wrong LED status - this was determined to be not of critical importance.

**IV. Nominal Performance**

_A. Purpose_

In this section the circuit is being tested under its nominal conditions (all component values at their nominal tolerances and temperature = 25 ̊C). The simulation demonstrates that the circuit correctly indicates air quality using two LEDs and switches at the intended 50% threshold.

_B. Parameters of Interest_

_Table 1. Nominal Values_

| **Parameter**                | **Symbol**       | **Target** | **Nominal Result** |
| ---------------------------- | ---------------- | ---------- | ------------------ |
| Threshold voltage            | V<sub>TH</sub>   | 1.65 V     | 1.64 V             |
| Trip Duty Cycle              | D<sub>trip</sub> | 50% ± 2%   | 49.8 %             |
| Red LED current (bad air)    | I(DLO)           | 2 mA       | 2 mA               |
| Green LED current (good air) | I(DHI)           | 1.5 mA     | 1.5 mA             |

_C. Simulation_

The nominal transient simulation was performed in LTspice with a 3.3 V supply. The PWM input source was configured with a 10kHz frequency and variable duty cycle to emulate the air quality sensor output. The simulation ran for 10 ms, with the key outputs being filtered voltage, NAND output, and LED currents, plotted to verify switching behavior.

Figure 2 Nominal Performance Simulation

_Transient simulation showing filtered PWM voltage (V(n003)), NAND output (V(out)), and LED currents I(DHI) and I(DLO)._

Figure 2 shows the nominal transient response of the air-quality indicator circuit. As the filtered PWM voltage (V(n003)) increases from 0 V to approximately 1.65 V, the NAND output (V(out)) transitions sharply from 3.3 V to 0 V. Before the transition, the red LED (DLO) conducts approximately 2 mA, indicating poor air quality. After the transition, the green LED (DHI) conducts about 1.5 mA, signifying good air quality. The switching threshold occurs at approximately 1.65 V, which corresponds to a 50 % duty-cycle signal from the air-quality sensor. The simulation confirms correct nominal performance and clear visual differentiation between air-quality states.

**V. Monte Carlo Analysis**

_A. Sensitivity to Component Tolerances_

_Purpose_

This section analyzes the sensitivity of the air-quality indicator circuit to realistic component tolerances. Using Monte Carlo simulation in LTspice, the effects of resistor, capacitor, and inductor variation were evaluated to determine how they impact the switching threshold and LED indication. The objective is to confirm whether the circuit maintains correct "good-air" and "bad-air" decisions under manufacturing variations.

_Table 2. Tolerances_

| Type                | Ohmic Range | Power Range | Tolerance | TempCo Range            |
| ------------------- | ----------- | ----------- | --------- | ----------------------- |
| LPF Series resistor | 1-10MOhms   | 0.125-2.5W  | 5%        | +/-50 > 200 ppm/Celcius |
| LPF Inductor        | ESR=1.2Ohms | 0.25W       | 5%        |                         |
| LPF capacitor       | ESR=0.1Ohms | N/A         | 5%        |                         |
| Pullup resistor     | 1-10MOhms   | 0.125-2.5W  | 5%        | +/-50 > 200 ppm/Celcius |
| Pulldown resistor   | 1-10MOhms   | 0.125-2.5W  | 5%        | +/-50 > 200 ppm/Celcius |

Table 2 summarizes the component types and tolerances used in this analysis. All resistors were assigned ±5% tolerance and ±200 ppm/°C tempco, consistent with standard E24 parts. The LPF inductor was given ±5% tolerance, and the LPF capacitor ±5%, reflecting typical small-signal ceramic capacitor and inductor variation. These values were implemented using LTspice's mc() function (ex: R1={mc(30,0.05)}), ensuring each Monte Carlo run generated a realistic component combination.

_Simulation_

A total of N = 200 Monte Carlo runs were performed at 25°C. Each run randomized the resistor, inductor, capacitor, and supply tolerances using the mc() function. A transient simulation was executed for each run while sweeping the PWM duty cycle around its nominal 50% threshold. The parameters of interest, LED currents and switching threshold voltage, were extracted using .meas statements:

.meas AC gain MAX mag(V(out)/V1)

.meas AC Low3dB WHEN mag(V(out)/V1)=gain/sqrt(2) Rise = 1

.meas AC High3dB WHEN mag(V(out)/V1)=gain/sqrt(2) Fall=1

Figure 3 Monte Carlo Sensitivity results for randomized component sets

The top plot shows the filtered PWM voltage, where small variations in the slopes indicate the expected tolerance effects in the LPF components (R1, L1, C1). The middle plot shows the NAND output, which transitions from high to low at slightly different times in each run. This spread represents the variation in switching threshold caused by resistor and capacitor tolerances in the NAND bias network. The bottom plot displays the LED currents for the green (DHI) and red (DLO) indicators. Although the exact switching instant varies between Monte Carlo samples, the behavior remains consistent: the green LED turns off and the red LED turns on once the filtered PWM voltage exceeds the threshold. These waveforms clearly demonstrate how component tolerances influence the threshold position but do not compromise the overall functionality of the air-quality indicator.

\_![A graph of a number of blue bars

AI-generated content may be incorrect.](data:image/png;base64,)Figure 4. Histogram of the forward voltage of diode D2, sampled at 4 ms for 60 Monte-Carlo runs at 25 °C using ±5% passive-component tolerances.\_

The measured D2 voltage varies over a narrow range from 0.5856 V to 0.5883 V, with a mean of approximately 0.5869 V. The distribution is tightly clustered and approximately symmetric, indicating that the circuit is only weakly sensitive to passive-component variation at the output LED node. Since the design specification requires an LED "ON" condition above 0.600 V, all Monte-Carlo realizations fall below that threshold, confirming that D2 remains OFF for this operating condition even with worst-case tolerance variation. This demonstrates that the diode output behavior is robust with respect to realistic manufacturing tolerances.

_B. Sensitivity to Temperature_

For the temperature-sensitivity portion of the Monte Carlo analysis, the circuit was simulated (Figure 1) across a wide operating range by sweeping the LTspice temperature setting from -25 °C to 85 °C in 10 °C increments. This range spans both commercial (0-70 °C) and industrial (-40-85 °C) temperature classes, ensuring the circuit is evaluated under realistic worst-case operating conditions. Resistor temperature coefficients, capacitor drift, diode forward-voltage variation, and transistor bias dependencies were all included through LTspice's TempCo modeling, allowing temperature effects on all major components to be captured accurately. A 60% PWM input was applied at each temperature step, representing the "greater-than-50%" operating case in which LED1 should turn ON and LED2 should turn OFF. Holding the duty cycle constant while sweeping temperature isolates how thermal behavior influences the switching threshold and LED output states. In Figure 1, the two LED outputs are on display, where the tolerances of every component are varied.![A computer screen shot of a graph

AI-generated content may be incorrect.](data:image/png;base64,)

_Figure 5. Pull-up LED D3 component-tolerance temperature test using a 60% PWM signal._

The pull-up LED is expected to turn ON in this condition, requiring its forward voltage to exceed 600 mV after the NAND output transitions. Across the full -25 °C to 85 °C sweep, all runs except two reach this threshold. The two failing cases occur at the highest temperatures (75 °C and 85 °C), where the reduced LED forward voltage at elevated temperature prevents the diode from reaching 600 mV. Lower temperature runs exceed the threshold easily, confirming stronger LED turn-on at colder conditions.![A graph of lines on a white background

AI-generated content may be incorrect.](data:image/png;base64,)

_Figure 6. LED D2 (output LED) component-tolerance temperature testing using a 60% PWM signal._

D2 is expected to begin ON (above 600 mV) and then turn OFF after the NAND output transition. Most temperature sweeps behave correctly, but the traces at 65 °C, 75 °C, and 85 °C fail to reach the 600 mV ON threshold at the start of the waveform. This is consistent with the expected reduction in LED forward voltage and transistor drive strength at higher temperatures. At lower temperatures, D2 reaches the ON threshold reliably, indicating correct operation in those conditions.
